newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria says it did not hinder Kurd murder inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Austria says it did not hinder Kurd murder inquiry.

text.p: Austria published a long-awaited report on Tuesday exonerating the government of colluding in the 1989 flight of suspected Iranian assassins, but opposition parties slammed the document as a whitewash.
Justice Minister Nikolaus Michalek presented the 200-page paper, compiled by the justice, interior and foreign ministries, at the cabinet's regular weekly meeting.
Copies were sent to parliamentary whips and the state prosecutor, who may use the report as a basis for his own, more thorough investigation.
"This is a good and open report by my ministry. There are no indications that political instructions impeded the murder inquiry," Interior Minister Karl Schloegl said.
His views were echoed by the other ministries involved in investigating the killing of Iranian Kurdish leader Abdorrahman Qasemlu and two other activists in Vienna eight years ago.

Opposition parties renewed their call for an independent parliamentary inquiry and said the papers failed to throw any light on the chain of events that led to the three suspected killers' escape to Iran.
Warrants for their arrest were issued only after they were outside the country.
"This report is not worth the paper it is written on," said Joerg Haider, leader of the far-right Freedom Party. "It is like asking a drunk driver to carry out his own breath test."
The liberals described the document as a smokescreen and said ministries could not be expected to give an objective assessment of their own actions. The environmentalist Greens suspected a cover-up.
"I fear that not all the facts have been put on the table and that this report will serve only to prevent the setting up of a parliamentary committee," Greens party leader Christoph Chorherr said.

Last week, the opposition forced an extraordinary parliamentary debate on allegations by senior diplomats and former Iranian president Abolhassan Bani-Sadr that Austrian ministers had bowed to economic and political pressure from Iran.

The ruling coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party, which has been in power for over a decade, used its parliamentary majority to vote down an opposition motion for a parliamentary inquiry.
The report confirmed that Iran had tried to exert pressure on the Austrian government but said it found no evidence that politicians had given way.
It conceded some mistakes in the investigation and communication break-downs between departments.
"It is always easier to recognise mistakes with the benefit of hindsight. We are taking measures to ensure that similar mistakes do not happen in the future," Schloegl said.
One of the most glaring errors -- a decision to drive one of the suspects to Vienna airport in an official motorcade -- was made by the justice ministry, according to security chief Michael Sika.
"In the eyes of the justice ministry this man was a witness and not a perpetrator. We were of a different opinion," Sika was quoted as saying in Der Standard newspaper.
